examples.problem_statement: Using the Multiplication using Working Base Method technique: multiply 251 \times 252 with a theoretical base of 1000 and a working base of 250. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.description: Fix the two bases the method runs on: the theoretical base 1000 and the working base 250, and note that 250 is 1000 divided by 4, so 4 is the division factor used later.
Subtract the working base from each multiplicand to get its deviation; both numbers sit above 250, so both deviations are positive.

solution.result: each number paired with its deviation
solution.description: Write the two numbers side by side with their deviations attached, which sets up the diagonal and vertical operations of the working base layout.
Do the diagonal addition: add either number to the other's deviation. Both diagonals give 253, which is the left-hand side of the raw answer.
Multiply the two deviations vertically; their product 2 becomes the right-hand side of the raw answer, giving the intermediate 253 | 2.
Because the working base is the theoretical base divided by 4, divide the LHS by that same factor 4; the division leaves a whole part 63 and a fractional part.
Convert the leftover fraction from the previous division back into units of the theoretical base by taking that fraction of 1000.
Add the converted fractional amount to the right-hand side, so the deviation product absorbs the remainder carried down from the LHS division.
Pad the right-hand side with leading zeros until it has as many digits as the theoretical base has zeros; 252 already fills the three places, so no zeros are added.
Join the LHS quotient 63 to the three-digit RHS 252 to read off the finished product.

examples.answer: 251 × 252 = 63252 using working base method with theoretical base 1000, working base 250, deviations +1 and +2, resulting in intermediate 253|2, then 63¼ quotient with fractional conversion 250 added to RHS to get 63252

key_reminders: Deviations are measured from the working base (250), not from the theoretical base.
When working base = theoretical base / n, the LHS must be divided by that same n.
A fractional remainder from the LHS division converts to that fraction of the theoretical base and is added to the RHS.
The RHS carries as many digits as the theoretical base has zeros.
common_mistakes: Writing the answer as 253252 by skipping the division of the LHS by 4.
Dropping the 1/4 remainder instead of converting it to 250 and adding it to the RHS of 2.
Padding the RHS to fewer than three digits, giving 6352 instead of 63252.

concept.technique_name: sentence-logic clue matching in text completion

examples.problem_statement: What readers most commonly remember about John Stuart Mill's classic exploration of the liberty of thought and discussion concerns the danger of (i) ______ : in the absence of challenge, one's opinions, even when they are correct, grow weak and flabby. Yet Mill had another reason for encouraging the liberty of thought and discussion: the danger of partiality and incompleteness. Since one's opinions, even under the best circumstances, tend to (ii) ______ , and because opinions opposed to one's own rarely turn out to be completely (iii) ______ , it is crucial to supplement one's opinions with alternative points of view. Blank (i): A tendentiousness, B complacency, C fractiousness. Blank (ii): D embrace only a portion of the truth, E change over time, F focus on matters close at hand. Blank (iii): G erroneous, H antithetical, I immutable.

solution.operation: Survey the passage and note that the first sentence is self-contained while the later sentences shift topic
solution.result: Blank (i) can be settled from sentence one alone
solution.description: Read the whole passage first to see how it divides: the opening sentence stands on its own, so the first blank is answerable before reading on, while the topic changes afterwards.

solution.operation: Read the colon after blank (i) as a signal that the following clause defines the blank
solution.result: The definition is 'in the absence of challenge, opinions grow weak and flabby'
solution.description: Use the punctuation clue: the colon announces that what follows names the very danger the blank labels, so the clause after it supplies the definition to match.

solution.operation: Match 'weak and flabby for want of challenge' against tendentiousness, complacency, fractiousness
solution.description: Test each first-blank option against that definition; unchallenged opinions make one complacent rather than tendentious or fractious, so complacency is the fit.

solution.operation: Read the next two sentences for the second danger Mill describes
solution.result: The theme is 'the danger of partiality and incompleteness'
solution.description: Scan forward to identify the controlling idea for the remaining blanks, which the passage states outright as partiality and incompleteness.

solution.operation: Fit blank (ii) to partiality: each person's opinion tends to embrace only a portion of the truth
solution.result: embrace only a portion of the truth (Choice D)
solution.description: Choose the second-blank option that expresses partiality itself, since that is the danger the sentence is explaining.

solution.operation: Fit blank (iii): opposing views are partially right, hence never completely erroneous
solution.description: Complete the parallel reasoning for the third blank, where saying opposing views are rarely completely wrong is what makes them worth consulting.

solution.operation: Reject E, F, H, I as dealing with change, immediacy, and antithesis
solution.result: Only B, D, G relate to partiality and incompleteness
solution.description: Eliminate the remaining options by showing that none of them touches the partiality-and-incompleteness theme that governs the second and third blanks.

examples.answer: Choice B: complacency; Choice D: embrace only a portion of the truth; Choice G: erroneous

key_reminders: A colon signals that the words after it define or explain the blank before it.
A self-contained opening sentence can be completed without reading the rest of the passage.
Later blanks are governed by the passage's explicitly stated theme, here 'partiality and incompleteness'.
common_mistakes: Choosing tendentiousness or fractiousness for blank (i), which describe combativeness rather than the flabbiness the colon defines.
Picking 'change over time' or 'focus on matters close at hand' for blank (ii), which address change and immediacy instead of partiality.
Picking 'antithetical' or 'immutable' for blank (iii) instead of the wrongness that 'rarely completely' negates.

examples.problem_statement: In the relative ordering diagram for this game, what is the earliest position that T could occupy?

solution.operation: Read off the elements the diagram places before T: X, S, and W
solution.result: X, S and W must all come before T
solution.description: Trace the ordering constraints back from T to collect every element that the diagram forces to precede it.

solution.operation: Three elements occupy the positions ahead of T, so T is pushed to position 3 + 1
solution.description: Count the forced predecessors and place T immediately after them, since three slots must be filled before T can appear.

key_reminders: Every element that a chain places before T must occupy an earlier slot than T.
The earliest slot for an element is one more than the count of elements forced to precede it.
common_mistakes: Answering 3RD by counting the predecessors X, S and W as the position number instead of the slots ahead of T.
